blocks.x: I want to make a note that the date is November 1st in All Saints Day in 1961 and we're over at 1109 South Galvez interviewing Mr. Fred Miner. Do you mind giving me your full name and also your nickname? How do you spell it?
Frederick C. Miner is my correct name. My nickname everybody call me H. A-C-H-I-E.
I used to say it was just like H, the letter H. That's what I thought it was, just like the letter H.
Do you mind telling just when you were born? I was born in 1913, December the 8th. What part of town? Right here in New Orleans? Right here in New Orleans on Perdita Street.
Perdita right there, not so far from this section here I guess. That's right, not too far.
Perdita what? Perdita between Roman and Bolivar.
Can you tell us anything about your family as much as you can remember about your parents? Did they play any musical instruments?
Well I had an uncle, I still have an uncle, and he was playing drums.
His name is Christopher Miner. Do you have his address or can you tell me?
At the present time I don't have his address, but he lives on Polgar between Claiborne and Durban. About two doors from Claiborne.
That's the young Polgar.
Between Claiborne and Durban.
And which side of the street? They're down?
They live on the uptown side.
Uptown. And a couple of doors from Claiborne. How is his health? Is he able to talk?
Oh yeah, he's still working. Still working and all, isn't he? Yeah, he's still working. How old is he about? He's around about 61 or 62.
That's not so old then. I thought maybe he'd be a little bit older.
No, he was about 61 or 62. That's all I know.

I know Professor Minetta talked about he used to play a few more years ago. Back in the old days in the district and all. That's right. The past is about 72 now. Yes. Or will be 72. I thought your uncle would be about that age. No, he's not that old. He's younger. I knew that he played drums. So we'll talk to him and get his story directly. Is that somebody at your door? Yes. If you want to stop any time, we can just turn this off. It doesn't have to be any special order or not. No. Did your father play any instruments?
No, my father didn't play anything.
Or mother?
Nobody but my uncle. That's the only one.
That's your uncle then. Did you have any brothers or sisters to play?
No brothers or sisters. Only one.
Did you tell us about your first instrument, what you started playing?
Well, I started to play in the ukulele. Ukulele.
Yeah, on the steps. How old were you then?
Well, I was around about 10 or 12 years old during that time. Then I picked up on a banjo. And I went to Son Thomas a little while. And then we started off in school. The Spasm Band.
Yeah. Son Thomas a banjo.
Banjo with Kidman A. Oh yeah.
I heard the name. I didn't remember it wrong. Yes.

Uh huh. And I left him and I went to Walter Preston a little while. Then after I could play Pretty Fair, John Kazimer, well we all from the same neighborhood, played with him. I played with Kid Clayton. Then I left them and went to Biloxi with the Spasm Band. We stayed over there during the summertime.
You might go into detail a little bit more about some of those bands. Like when you played with John Kazimer, who else was in the band?
Well, during that time they had a fella I know by the name of Wooden Joe. Oh yeah, sure.
I remember him.
And they had Carnish on the trombone. Oh yeah. And uh, every now and then I would see Bob Lyons with him, but Joe Gabriel would play mostly with him at the time, during that time.
I see Joe Gabriel played bass.
Joe Gabriel played bass.
Yeah. We talked to Clarence, wasn't it Gabriel? That's Clarence Gabriel. Is there any kid that Clarence is in place in there?
No, I don't think so. No relation to that family?

No, I don't think so because I don't know. August Linwall's wife is the Gabriel's, yes. They came from up, stay around Thibodeau or something like that. Do you remember where your, what was your very first job that you played? Do you remember that you ever got paid for? Was there even with any other band when you started out?
The first job I played, I played with a piano player and uh, that was the first time I ever played on a job, the first time, just with a piano player. You remember that job?
With your banjo.
With the banjo, yeah, with the banjo.
Do you remember what was that age?
Somewhere out in Bacchanal Boulevard.
Was it the private party or something else?
Private party, private party.
Who was the piano player, remember?
Uh, George White. No, you don't know him. Still around?
It's Leon Mumford's brother. Who? Remember Leon Mumford the piano? Yeah, yeah. His brother.
Oh yeah. Um, did you all have any regular jobs with the, say that Kazmer band we were talking about?
No, we didn't have any regular jobs, just spotting around, that's all. I spotting around with Clayton too.
About how, when was that? You were born in 1913, you see?
Yeah, that was around about 1929 or 30 when it started. It started off. Then after I left them, then I started with Hande, John Hande. Yeah, remember who else?
Louisiana Shakers. Yeah, that was Louisiana Shakers.
Oh yeah. And he was the leader then?
He was the leader then.
Was he playing Faraday then or his alto?
No, he was still playing his alto.

Do you remember who else was in the band? The other? Well during that time they had Rickard on the trumpet, Alexis Rickard, Willie Paggio and Dukangi that was playing the trumpet. Morris French was playing trombone.
Did he use more than one cover? It was a big band? Yeah, it was a big band.
Yeah, big band. They had ten pieces.
Oh yeah.
And Morris French was on the trombone, Roy Evans was on the drums, Old Man Kimball was on the bass, and Hande was on the sax, George Clark and Edward Botley, and myself on the band.
It was two good siblings, George Clark and Edward Botley was talking about.
Oh, speaking of Botley, the old timers tell about this. Buddy Botley used to go up in the airplane, I mean in the balloon.
No, this was a little younger. No relation at all. No relation. No relation.
He lived over on the Gravier of Perdido along in that section, near the old Simon Call along in there. So I just wondered, no relation. No relation.
Then I left Hande's band, I went with Walter Pichon's band, and we played for Mamie Smith on the Vaudeville shows.
What was the blues singer? Blue singer. Who was on that band with drumming?
In that band, Thedo Poinel was on sax, George Clark was on sax, and Botley again was on sax, Edward Botley. Chester Zardes on bass.
Chester Zardes on bass.

Chester Zardes on bass. Stanley Williams on drum. Bigfoot Bill was on drum. And Pichon was on the piano. I was playing the band, and Clifford Brown on trumpet, Gordette was on trumpet. That's Clifford Brown. Oh yes. And we had a boy from out of town playing trombone. Can't remember his name. That was?
Trombone.
Yeah, he could play a lot of trombone.
I think his last name was Meredith.
Yeah. And that was with Mamie Smith. About what year? Can you figure out if it was during the depression?
Oh yeah, that was during the depression time. I didn't know what happened to her. I didn't know what happened to her. I never. Well, I didn't hear that she was. She settled in New York.
And I think married some fellow. Evidently had a lot of money and settled down on riverside drive or someplace up the river

there. Real nice place. I didn't hear that for around 1940. You hadn't been with her so long before that. No. It was around that. It was around that. It was around that. Yeah. It was around that. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. It was around 30, 36 or 35, something like that. Yeah.
I didn't know that she was still active then because she made those real early records. Yes. About 1922 or 1925, I think she stopped recording. I thought maybe she just retired. I don't know.
That was around, that was around 35, 36.
Yeah. When she came down.
That's right there.
Right there.
Yeah.
Right there.
Yeah. That was Mamie.
Yeah.
Mamie's Mamie.
Where did you travel? Yeah. We played mostly all of the southern states. We left from here and went to Memphis and Nashville and Georgia.
Was it a whole show or just a show up here in Vaudeville?
No. She had a whole show with her.
Do you remember the old T-O-B-A? T-O-B-A or something? T-O-B-A.
T-O-B-A. Yeah.
T-O-B-A.
Was it the book of them? No, it was after that. After that. After that.
I knew they had that Vaudeville circuit and all that.
That's right.

It was right after that. I knew they had to travel on that like Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith did. I never didn't know what happened to Mamie. How did she sound in person? Because her records were so old.
Well, she really sound good during that time. She did really good. She had a number she used to sing, Golf and Papa. Yeah. She really could sing that.
I can't remember all of her record titles, but she made something so old and awful like that. Well, we did pretty fair.
While I was with her, we did pretty fair during them times. How was her voice?
Was it a deep or high voice? She had a nice voice.
Was it a deep or high voice? She had no, sort of a deep voice. Deep.
Yeah. And the record that doesn't sound as full is Bessie Smith. It sounds like a lighter voice than some. It seemed pretty heavy and all that.
Well, her voice seemed pretty heavy.
It might have gotten that way in the older days.
Older days, yes.
The Blanche songs, don't you have the kind of voice like that? Yes. Something like Blanche. Yeah, something like Blanche. Yeah, something like Blanche. Yeah, something like Blanche.
Yeah, something like Blanche.
Yeah, something like Blanche. Yeah, something like Blanche. That's why I asked him. Yeah. This is a pretty big orchestra then. There's been weather all this. Oh, yes. How was the girl artist then?
We had about 10 pieces about every day. Because we had a song star also with us.
Did you appear in regular theaters or was it a 10-hour?
Yeah, regular, no, regular theaters. Regular theaters. Regular theaters.
What's that boy's name, a singer with y'all?
Sidney Hansel.
Yeah, he's running this place in Port Supper right now. That's right, yeah. Keep him here? Yeah.
Yeah, Sidney is familiar.
He's been working out there for many, many years after you know what. Out there at the place I think he cooked. He could sing good.
Sidney Hansel?
Hansel. H-A-N-S-E-L.
Hansel. I might have heard of him. What type of songs did he sing? Mostly blues or other ballads?
No, he sang mostly ballad songs during that time.
How long did you stay with that?

Well, we stayed with Mamet about six or seven months. And the band broke up and came on back home. And then I went with Celestan's band. I stayed on the road with Celestan's band about a year. Who did Celestan live then? Well, Bill Matthews was on the trombone. John Poodle was on the bass. Anderson, uh, Anderson's, what's his name? Andy Anderson. Andy Anderson playing trumpet. Holloway was on the trumpet. And, uh, we had that boy from Tuy. From what? I think he's from around, uh, around the home or somewhere. Trumpet. No, Anderson, Holloway, and Celestan. That's right. That's the three, Celestan. Oh, that's three of them.
That's after God fell asleep.
Yeah. And I had taken Kimball's place.
Oh, was that, um...
That was during, right during the Depression time. The mailman. No, that's right. The mailman. That's the time when he went on the PWA I had taken his place.
He played over the, across the street from us the other night.
The other night, yeah.
First time I guess I heard him play him. I might have heard him before, I'm not sure.
Yeah, it was good banjo player. He played bass too. Yeah, he played bass and banjo.
And John Porter was on the piano.

The sousaphone, yes. Mm-hmm. And, uh, we had a K2 on the piano. And, uh, there were two drummers at that time who was with the band. Was that a big K2? Yeah, no, Lil K2. He was in California now. And, uh, had Lil Gord at one time in Lawrence. I don't know if they were both named, but they were playing drums. Each one of them taking the place during the time when I was in the band. Oh. Well, at that time I had switched over to guitar then. The Chinese had left already. Oh yeah, the Chinese had left.
Yeah, so there's a new bunch. And, uh, where did you, did you all travel? A good deal.
I know you usually travel a lot. Yeah, we did a lot of traveling. And went all around Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Texas.
I've heard it sometime in the later days that Salisand had two bands. Did he have two in those days? Like one on the road one?
Well, no, he didn't have one band at that time. One band. That was before he went in the paddock. Yeah.
Before. Yeah. Did he did. Do you remember having two bands? One on the road one there? No, I don't remember that. Some people say he talked like he had two of them. Why?
No, during the time I was with him, he was with the band. He was always with the band. He was always with the band.
Because he would tell them, sometime before he sent them for his job, he would tell the people that he can't play it. Yeah.
So I wondered, because some people said, oh, they called one the society band. Like these people.

But here's what they must have been thinking about, you see. You see, when Salisand Ridley broke up, we had Riznitz tuxedo, and Salisand's tuxedo, you see, because I was on the road with Riznitz tuxedo in the 20s. Yeah, that may be what I heard then. Yeah, that's what I heard. Me, Emma, Barry, Gilbert, Young, my brother Leo, and this trombone player I was telling you about that stayed dressed up all the time. We all changed clothes, you know, right on the road, and he'd stay dressed up just in his tuxedo suit. And when we'd get out the bus, we'd go change clothes and everything, and he still didn't look no better than he looked. Yeah, I mean, he stayed clean all the time.
That's how he did it. Yeah, it's hard to do.
Well, that's what must have happened. They were two tuxedos, you see. It was Riznitz tuxedo and Salisand's tuxedo.
See, that's what happened. It might have been on the late days that he was sent out on the- stuff

band of the job he couldn't take. Couldn't take. Maybe so. He sent some people out someplace. People think it was his band, but without him. Well, let's see. After Celestan, then, is there anything else to tell about Celestan's band? You always played the banjo, I know.
Yeah, I always played the banjo.
I wonder, did you ever play guitar?

Well, I started my guitar along with Celestan's band, but I had the banjo, too. And after I left Celestan's band, well, I came back and I joined P. Ron's band. Then I was playing a straight guitar with P. Ron's band. We went on the boat and brought the boat up to St. Louis one season. That was our last season on the boat. And after I left P. Ron's band, well, I came and joined Joe Rogashio's band. That was a 16-piece band.
Did you make any of those records?
No, I never did make a record with Joe.
You kind of made some vocabulary records.
Well, during the time I was supposed to make the records, I had my money up for the records and for the transportation. We was going to New York. He had a six-piece band then.
Yeah.
And I left his band to go with P. Sean's band. That was a little six-piece band he had then.

Anything else about this band that P. Ron had? I remember I was up in Missouri, I think 1936 and 1937 along there. I remember seeing that boat advertisement that they advertised, the P. Ron band. And I didn't get...
You didn't get a chance to see it.
They didn't stop at our town, but a nearby town, Wednesday, Illinois would advertise it. And I wondered...
Well, we was on the three of them. We played the Capitol, the GS, and the President.
Oh, yeah. I remember all those boats. Who was all in the band?

During that time, Leo Dejean, Joe Phillips, Eddie Pearson. Oh, yeah. And Eddie Pearson. And it was trombone. And saxophone was Louis Cartrell, Oscar Rouson, and Elliot Taylor. On the drums was Sidney Montague, Booker, Booker Washington on bass, Lewis Gibbons on piano, and I was playing the straight guitar.
Any electric guitar in those days?
Well, not on the boat, because, I mean, you could get an amplifier built for that AC and DC current.
Yeah, DC, I remember.
Yes. But I didn't have that. I just had a straight regular guitar.
You like guitar or banjo best?
Well, both of them's good if you can play them.
Yeah.
And I wish I could play either one of them.
Sounds all right to me. Yeah. The one you make the most money with, that's the best one.
That's the best one. Right. Seemed like the Badger is making the most money right now.
Yeah. It's back popular again. Popular. Yeah. In the small Dixieland bands and all. I was going to ask about the other instruments, what else you took up in the late years in the brass band. Yeah.
Well, I had a trumpet. I have a trumpet around and I kind of play a couple of tunes or so on it.
I heard you out on a parade.
Not too good, but the trumpet.
I don't know about it. I understand. You can't be good on everything. That's right. Some practices played that. Yeah. That's right. Yeah. Notice the bass drum and all here in the room here. Did you?
No. That belonged to my sons. They played.
Your brothers never played the drums. No. I never played the drums. The piano? Anybody in your family played the piano?
My little boy played the piano. My little boy played the piano.
My little boy played the piano.
My little boy played the piano.
Is there anything else about the boat? Do you remember what year it was? I don't remember when I saw those ads. It must have been about the same season.
The last season. The last season. Around the last season. That should have been around about in the 40s.
It could have been that late then. Yes.
That late.
I used to go home to Missouri almost every year. It could have been that late. Before the war.
Yeah. It was before the war.
Before the war.
Before the war. Because when the war came out, I remember I went with Sidney Desvins band. Oh, yeah. See. And I stayed with Sidney Desvins band until after the war.
Yeah.
Then I went with Paul Barberand.
Sidney Desvins had a big band.
Yeah.
I remember that.
I probably heard you with them maybe once or twice. Didn't know you in those days. To get back to Pierone's band, do you remember how far up the river you went?

Well, I didn't go no further than St. Louis with the band. St. Louis. That's the furthest I went with the band. But they had made trips all around Minneapolis. Yes, they went on Central, Minnesota. Well, I saw them advertising.
They went to Quixey, Illinois, or Kyrgyz, Iowa, or Hannibal, Missouri. That's right. I went on there. I went on by. Did you all sleep on the boat then?
Yeah, we slept on the boat down there in the bottom in the hall or something like that. That's where our sleeping quarters was.
Did you ever play on the boat when they got back to New Orleans here?
Yes, we stayed on the boat during the whole summer season mostly. Before Easter Monday, the boat would leave out.
Yeah, go up north. Yes.

But I wasn't fortunate enough to get that trip. I got it on the last when things was going down there. Because we played here one season, and that last season we were taking the boat up to St. Louis, and that was all.
Did you ever play any other jobs at Pierone around here?
Well, yes, I stayed with Pierone's band, I'd say about two years or better. 41. Yes.
What did he call it then?
A.J. Pierone. Yeah, that's right. Own name on the band.
That's right. Did he use Sidney Montague to stay on drums?
Sidney Montague was playing drums during that time.
Way after Cottrell's time.
Oh, the old man. Yeah, that was after his time.
Yeah, he had a complete different band.
Yeah. Complete change, man. Complete change in the band.
In the old days, you'd have Peter Bogaj. Peter Bogaj.
Tio. Tio. Charlie Bogaj playing banjo. Albert Oney Grand Alto, saxophone.
There's a picture. Several pictures of that band has been printed. Some of them have been printed.
Steve Lewis playing piano.
Yeah. Yeah. You ever worked with Steve Lewis?
No, I've never worked with Steve.
I never even got the hearing plane.
Never worked with Steve.
Except on records, you did make some records.
People, the people you'd be crazy about. Oh, yeah. I'd go with Tio on Saturday night sometimes and people crowd around. I don't care. I don't like that, huh?
Let's see. Anything else you can tell about Sidney Desby's band? Where did you work?

Well, we worked all around New Orleans with Sidney's band because we never did leave out of time with the band. We played mostly all the dances was in New Orleans at that time. It was during the war time.
I remember them too. I think they played San Jacinto club. That's right. San Jacinto, just the T-Rome. Just the T-Rome, too. Yeah. That's right. I remember that. I heard them at the San Jacinto.

We used to play two bands at the Gypsy. Yeah, at the Gypsy band. Yeah. I had a mixed band. Yeah. Yeah, I was in the neighborhood. We used to have two bands on Sunday evening. Do you remember the members of Sidney's band on the Fairroom?

Let's see now. Joe Phillips was on trumpet. Alvin Alcorn on trumpet. And Sidney's on trumpet. Eddie Pearson was on trombone. And I forgot the fellow's other name from Cross the River. He was on trombone, too. He wrote. To trombone. No, not the Rooks. Brownskin boy, collecting insurance.
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. We met him one time. I can't think of his name. And I told you he was a very fine trombone player.
Yeah, fine trombone player he was.
Handsome looking boy. Yeah. I remember now. Oh, he was a good trombone player. He's collecting insurance over the river. That's right, yeah. If you ever see Peter Bocai after action.
He can tell him about that. Yeah.
He played with Sidney Daphne. Yeah. Very good trombone player. He played with Walter Pichon.
Now, how old is he? He's a fairly young fellow.
Oh, yeah, he's young. He's in his studies.
That's all. Yeah. And who else?
Yeah, on the saxophone, we had Cottrell, Oscar Ruzon, Sam Lee. And in the rhythm section was William Houston and Louis Barbaran.
I'm trying to think who was playing bass with us then.

I can't think of the bass player. Rain was playing at that time, playing bass. And I was playing the guitar. Kimball was playing the bass. That's right. Young Kimball. That was the band then. And we stayed with that band about three or four years with Sidney's. And left them. Then I went and got Kimball, Louis Barbaran, Alvin Alcorn, and myself with the full tunes.
With four?
Just four of us, yes.
You're singing all up here?
Oh, yeah, sing.
Sounds like a good night singing. Where did you play? Any special longer engagements?

Well, we just played all engagements around town. We would play after the bands or before the bands would come. Like Louis Armstrong, King Cole. And those bands would come in during that time to play dances, concert, and we would fill in a standby group.

I was going to ask something about the old-time banjo players. When you were a boy, even before you took up music or maybe even wanted to take up music, can you remember the very earliest music you ever heard? What kind of...
Well, during that time, the bands, they all used to be on the truck.
Yeah.
And I can remember Rene and they had Guy Kelly during that time. I think he was playing on the truck. I know Punch was around. Georgie Boy, because he stayed about three or four doors for me.
Clarinet.
Clarinet.
That's right. I know he lived over on Perdido Street. I met his wife there once. She still lived there.
He stayed about three or four doors for me.
Fifteen years ago.
Yeah, I know...
How was he? How did he sound? I never got to hear him or meet him or...
Well, all I know, they could play that and it just sounded good to me then. Yeah, they all could play.
He used to have banjo or guitar in the wagon in those days?
Well, he used to have banjos. Banjos. Banjos. Banjos, yeah.

You know, Georgie Boy could talk to you in the clarinet, you know? He'd talk to his hands and his clarinet. Really? Yeah. He used to like it in his voice? We used to play with Guy at the Willow Inn. I remember he used to send John Kazmin nights that he had to work, you know, somewhere. Yeah.
Who were some of the best banjo players when you were just coming up, when you were starting to learn? Or who did you like to hear?

Well, they had some real good banjo players after I started learning how to play banjo. Because during that time, Walter Preston, Kit Thomas, and Bocas, they were the kind of banjo players that the fellas started playing a little later on. Because the fellas a little later on started playing the solo banjos. Now, Kimball, used to admire him the way he played because he used to put the banjo behind his neck and play.
Well, now you have a chance, I guess.
Well, I went to lesson with Sales. And Rene Hall was here then.
Yeah, I agree.
And Dijon, Ferdinand Dijon, he was here. And there was a little fella named Walter Williams. He was playing banjo. Son, Duh, is Danny Barker.
Oh, is that him?
That's Son, Duh, Danny Barker.
Son, Duh?
I don't know if I heard of you.

Yeah, Son, Duh, that's what they called him. Maybe I've heard of him. I haven't seen Danny for so long, you forget about him being from here. And then we had a fine banjo player with us, Harry Faggert.
Harry Faggert, he was across the lake, though.
He was just there. Yeah.
Well, during them times, they had nothing but good banjo players there.
There wasn't a lot of them.
That's right.
You remember the time when you had a good wrist and everything. Yeah.
Yeah, them banjo players was out there. Gee whee.
Do you remember when the banjo first came in? Or I guess when you were a boy, it was already popular?
I was already popular when I came in.
In the real old days, they used guitar mostly.
Well, yeah, I understood because I heard his record by Louis Armstrong with his Hot 5 during them times. Johnny Sincere was playing the guitar. They didn't have no banjos then, I don't remember.
You didn't mention one of the very best, Marrero.
John Marrero.
John Marrero.
Yes.
George Dino talks a lot about him. He's his favorite, I believe, in those days. He talks about a couple others, too.
AJ, did you remember Caffrey?
No.
I don't know anybody. Yeah, well, maybe he was a model. I had never seen him.
Percy, all right. Percy Sevier.
I put Sevier.
Do you remember him?
I'm taking lessons from him, too. He came from Mississippi. I think Jackson.
Whatever happened to him? Do you remember?
Well, I don't know what happened to him, but during the time he was playing with Sidney Desvins' band, when I heard him.
Yeah, he was a good banjo. Yeah, he must have been.
Oh, yeah, he was really good.
Yeah.
Well, during that time, they had a lot of banjo players.
That boy, Lucent Johnson, he wasn't from here, but he stayed here a lot. That was Harry Pettiford's brother.
Yeah.
Boy, he could play some time.
That's what I'm saying. Then that time we had banjo players around there, they could play like Rene Hall.
Yeah, Rene Hall. Sills. Sills, Rene Hall.
Yeah, they were playing there.
Where's that? Daniel. That's right. Yeah, they were playing that banjo there. Kimball. That's a bunch of better banjo. Joyce Gannon.
That's right. But the guitar took it, taking everything away from him.
It started playing the guitar.
Yeah, I guess they all switched back to guitar. Did you have regular lessons when you learned?

Yeah, I had regular lessons when I learned, because I went to Kimberl, like I said, for lessons, regular music lesson. Then I went to Sills, I also went to Poissy. Trying to learn a little bit from each other, each and every one of them.
Do you remember some of the earliest parades that you were going, what the parades were like? Did you ever follow them?

Well, I couldn't follow the parades, but I seen a lot of parades though. I seen a lot of old musicians in the parade bands playing too. In fact, I knew them all, because I was right around the corner from the Dewey Club and the Tulane Club.
What was the other club?
Dewey. Dewey. How do you remember? D-E-W-E-Y-S. Deweys. That was on Roman, between Perdida and Gravia. Oh yeah, right there that you're laying there.
Right around the corner.
Right around the corner from the Tulane.
It's pouring down a little now, I guess.
No, it's still there, but they made a large house out of it.
Well, really?
I'll have to go and take a picture. Yes, a large house there.
What was that, an organization? A social pleasure club?
Yeah, it was a social pleasure club. That's where Louis Armstrong and them used to play those fumes from.

Yeah, I didn't know that place. It's on Roman between... Between Perdida and Gravia. And where's the big church, the big cathedral or whatever it is in there? You talking about St. Joseph? St. Joseph.
St. Joseph at Tulane and Roman. Yeah. And the Tulane Club is on Gravia in there, Roman. And this is on Roman between Gravia and Perdida. Oh, yes.
